members.title: File descriptor from mkstemp leaks if fchmod/fdopen raises before the with-block takes ownership
members.problem: `fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(...)` returns a raw OS file descriptor. If `os.fchmod(fd, 0o600)` (or `os.fdopen(fd, "w")` itself) raises OSError before the `with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as f:` block takes ownership of `fd`, the except branch only does `os.unlink(tmp_path)` — it never closes `fd`. Since a raw int fd has no `__del__` to reclaim it, this leaks a file descriptor on every failure of that early step.
source_window: # M1: set 0600 on the temp fd BEFORE writing or replacing, so the final file
members.why_it_matters: In a long-running daemon, repeated reset-token-file failures (e.g. a permissions issue on the config volume) would silently exhaust file descriptors over time, eventually causing unrelated I/O failures across the app.
members.fix_hint: Wrap the fchmod call in its own try/except that explicitly `os.close(fd)` before re-entering the outer handling, or move `os.fchmod` to apply via `os.fdopen(fd, "w")` first so the context manager always owns the fd.

fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, suffix=".tmp")
try:

    with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as f:
        ...

members.title: mkstemp sits outside the try, so a failed temp-file create returns a 500 and breaks the non-fatal promise
members.problem: `tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, ...)` runs before the `try:` block. If the config volume is read-only, full (ENOSPC) or not writable (EACCES), the OSError skips the handler that is meant to swallow it. It escapes through `run_in_executor` into `reset_request_post`, which raises after the token has already been minted and logged. The docstring and the D-17 comments say a file-write failure must not be fatal, but the operator gets a 500 instead of the neutral confirmation.
source_window: # M1: set 0600 on the temp fd BEFORE writing or replacing, so the final file
members.why_it_matters: On a read-only or full config volume, which is a real NAS setup, the recovery endpoint shows an error page even though a token was minted. The operator may think recovery failed.
members.fix_hint: move mkstemp inside the try (initialize fd/tmp_path to None) so the OSError handler covers it

members.title: tempfile.mkstemp call sits outside the try/except OSError, violating the documented non-fatal guarantee
members.problem: The function's docstring explicitly promises OSError is caught and never re-raised ("D-17: in-memory token is the authority... Do NOT re-raise"), but `tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, suffix=".tmp")` is called BEFORE the `try:` block. mkstemp can raise OSError subclasses (PermissionError, FileNotFoundError if the config dir is missing, OSError for ENOSPC/EMFILE), and none of those are caught here.
members.why_it_matters: This function is awaited via run_in_executor in reset_request_post with no surrounding try/except, so an uncaught OSError here propagates into the request handler and turns what the code explicitly documents as a non-fatal file-write failure into an unhandled 500, even though the token was already minted and logged successfully.
members.fix_hint: Move the `tempfile.mkstemp` call inside the try block (or wrap it in its own try/except OSError) so the stated non-fatal guarantee actually holds for every failure mode of acquiring the temp file.

findings.title: File descriptor leaks when os.fchmod fails before os.fdopen takes ownership
findings.problem: The raw fd from mkstemp is only handed to a closing context manager at `os.fdopen`. If `os.fchmod(fd, 0o600)` raises OSError (EPERM is common on CIFS/SMB or some NFS mounts), control goes to the except branch. That branch unlinks tmp_path but never calls `os.close(fd)`, and the finally only closes dir_fd. The whole scope is in view and no close happens on this path.
findings.fix_hint: track whether fdopen took ownership and os.close(fd) in the except/finally when it did not
findings.why_it_matters: On a filesystem that rejects fchmod, each reset request leaks one fd in the long-running daemon. The 60s rate limit slows this down but does not stop it.
source_window: # M1: set 0600 on the temp fd BEFORE writing or replacing, so the final file
# is already 0600 after os.replace with no post-rename chmod window.

findings.title: Unauthenticated reset request waits on search_lock, which search cycles hold for their whole network run
findings.problem: `reset_request_post` takes `app.state.search_lock`. `make_search_job` (scheduler.py:131-226) holds that lock for an entire search cycle, including all Radarr/Sonarr HTTP calls. While a cycle runs, the reset request hangs until it finishes and can hit client or proxy timeouts. Requests that pass the optimistic pre-lock check also pile up on the lock. The lock is only needed to guard the rate-limit and reset_token state, which the search cycle never touches.
findings.fix_hint: guard last_reset_time/reset_token with a dedicated reset lock, not search_lock
findings.why_it_matters: A locked-out operator may see the reset request hang or time out whenever a slow search cycle is running.

members.title: Unauthenticated reset request waits on the global search_lock, which search cycles hold for their whole run
members.problem: The handler takes `app.state.search_lock`. Scheduled search jobs hold that lock for an entire cycle, including HTTP calls to Radarr and Sonarr (scheduler.py:131-226). A reset request that arrives mid-cycle hangs until the cycle ends. The timestamp is only written inside the lock (routes.py:1656), so the optimistic check at 1647 lets every concurrent unauthenticated request through and they all queue on the lock with no bound. The only state guarded here is `last_reset_time` and `reset_token`, which do not need to be serialised against search cycles.

members.title: Password reset token logged in cleartext, bypassing the project's secret-redaction sink
members.problem: Global CLAUDE.md (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), Security section (marked absolute, taking precedence over all other conventions): 'Never log sensitive data (passwords, tokens, PII, auth headers).' The new `reset_request_post` handler mints a password-reset token and logs its raw value via `logger.warning("Password reset token minted. Read from 'docker logs' or reset-token.txt: {token}", token=token)`. This is an unqualified rule and the violating line is fully visible and unambiguous -- the code's own comments (routes.py:1681-1686) confirm it is deliberate ('the warning log line INCLUDES the token value') and that the token is intentionally excluded from the codebase's existing redaction mechanism ('intentionally NOT added to collect_secrets / the redacting sink (unlike session_secret/password_hash)').
source_window: # D-17: log line first, THEN file write — so a file-write failure still leaves the
"Password reset token minted. Read from 'docker logs' or reset-token.txt: {token}",
members.why_it_matters: A password-reset token is a credential that grants account takeover; logging it in cleartext means it persists indefinitely in `docker logs` output and in any log aggregator/shipper the operator has configured, well beyond the file's 0600/config-volume boundary, and bypasses the project's own established redaction mechanism (triggarr/startup.py:74-98, `collect_secrets()`) used for every other secret (password_hash, session_secret, api_key).
members.fix_hint: Drop the token from the log message (log only that a token was minted and where to find it, e.g. 'see reset-token.txt'); the 0600 reset-token.txt file already carries the value for operator recovery, so the log line doesn't need to duplicate it in cleartext.
members.current_code:
logger.warning(
    "Password reset token minted. Read from 'docker logs' or reset-token.txt: {token}",
    token=token,
)

members.title: Reset token leaks into HTTP-rendered log viewer, contradicting the code's own "never in an HTTP response" invariant
members.problem: The new code mints a CSPRNG reset token and logs it in plaintext via `logger.warning("...: {token}", token=token)` (routes.py:1689-1692), with an explicit comment asserting 'The token MUST NOT appear in any HTTP response' and that this is 'the ONLY log line that will ever contain the token value', deliberately excluded from `collect_secrets`/the redacting sink (triggarr/logging.py's `create_redacting_sink`). That assumption is false: `setup_logging()` (triggarr/logging.py) also registers a second sink, `buffer_sink`, which captures every log record at or above the configured level (default `log_level='info'`, models/config.py:125, so WARNING passes) into the process-wide `log_buffer` (triggarr/log_buffer.py) WITHOUT any redaction filter applied (the redaction list only contains `collect_secrets()` output, which excludes the reset token by design). `log_buffer.get_recent(30)` is then rendered directly into HTTP responses by two existing, unmodified routes: `GET /` (dashboard, routes.py:382) and `GET /partials/log-viewer` (routes.py:1083), via `triggarr/templates/partials/log_viewer.html` which prints `{{ entry.message }}` verbatim (HTML-escaped, but the secret value itself is fully present in the page text). Both routes require authentication (middleware.py's EXEMPT_PREFIXES do not cover `/` or `/partials/log-viewer`), so this is not reachable pre-auth, but it means ANY authenticated web session — a strictly lower, different trust boundary than the 'operator-only' channels the code intends (docker host/SSH access to read `docker logs`, or filesystem access to read the 0600 `reset-token.txt`) — can read the live reset token for up to 15 minutes (its TTL) or until it rolls out of the 200-entry ring buffer, simply by loading the dashboard or polling the htmx log-viewer partial (which auto-refreshes every 5s). An attacker who obtains any authenticated session (stolen cookie, XSS elsewhere in the app, shared/logged-in browser) can thereby read the reset token and use it (once /reset/confirm is wired up) to set a new password, creating a persistence mechanism that survives revocation of the original session — something the 'operator-only sinks' design was specifically trying to prevent.
source_window: # D-17: log line first, THEN file write — so a file-write failure still leaves the
"Password reset token minted. Read from 'docker logs' or reset-token.txt: {token}",
members.why_it_matters: The whole security rationale for logging the token (vs. e.g. emailing it) is that 'docker logs' and the config-volume file require host-level access distinct from the web application's own session/auth boundary. Because the existing in-memory log buffer captures the same message and an unmodified dashboard route renders it, that boundary is silently collapsed: a compromised or borrowed web session becomes sufficient to self-service a password reset, regardless of host access controls.
members.fix_hint: Either route this log line through a sink that is excluded from log_buffer capture (e.g. add a `extra`/filter flag the buffer_sink checks and skips), or add the reset token to a redaction list applied to buffer_sink specifically (even though it's intentionally excluded from the stderr redacting sink), so the token cannot reach `log_buffer`/the web log viewer while still appearing in `docker logs`.

    token=token,
)

members.title: Plaintext reset token written to general application log stream (docker logs)
members.problem: Separate from sec-001, the token is written in plaintext to the primary stderr log stream consumed by `docker logs`. This is a documented, deliberate design decision (inline comments reference specific prior design decisions D-02/RESEARCH #4), treating docker-log access as equivalent to host/filesystem access (the same trust level as the 0600 token file written right after). No evidence in this diff shows the deployment forwards docker logs to a third party (log aggregator, support bundle, centralized logging) with broader retention or access than the local host, so I cannot demonstrate exposure beyond the intended operator boundary.
